notes.b: Athletics is a group of running, jumping, throwing and walking events. Each can be measured, both against the performer's own ability and against standards set by other people's achievements.
points: The events may be performed indoors or outdoors, so the same event can be contested in a hall or on an outdoor track or field.
Performance is judged by the measurement itself: a time for running events, and a distance or height for throwing and jumping events. No opinion is needed to decide a result.
Progress is shown by comparing a performance with the performer's own earlier results and with the achievements of others, which is why athletics suits both self-improvement and competition.
Walking events are named in the definition of athletics, but the events a learner can choose for assessment are running, throwing and jumping.
notes.tip: Mention walking events only when you define athletics. The categories and events you choose from are running, throwing and jumping.

notes.h: The three categories and their events
notes.b: Athletics events fall into three categories: running, throwing and jumping. You need to know which events belong to each category, because the assessment is chosen from one of them.
points: Running events: sprints (short, flat-out races), middle distance, long distance and hurdles.
Sprints: 100 m, 200 m and 400 m.
Middle distance: 800 m and 1500 m.
Long distance: 5000 m, 10,000 m and beyond.
Hurdles: the hurdles events, each run over a row of barriers that the athlete must clear while racing.
Throwing events: shot-put (a heavy ball pushed from the shoulder), discus, javelin and hammer. In each, an implement (the object thrown) is sent as far as possible.
Jumping events: high jump (clear a bar for height), long jump and triple jump (both for distance).
notes.tip: Technique for each event is taught in the notes for its own category, so here you only need the lists of events.

notes.h: The choice rule for the performance assessment
notes.b: You do not assess the whole of athletics. The syllabus narrows the choice in two steps, first a category and then a single event within it.
points: The learner selects one category: running, throwing or jumping.
Within that category, so as to keep the assessment manageable, the performance assessment (the practical assessment of how well you perform) focuses on one activity, for example the discus.
The assessment covers the skills and techniques, the tactics (decisions made to perform better), and the rules and safe practice of that one activity.
notes.tip: Remember the order: one category first, then one event inside it, such as the discus within throwing.

notes.b: Athletics results are objective, so a performer's improvement can be recorded and compared exactly.
points: A running time or a throwing or jumping distance is recorded by a timekeeper, electronic timing or a field judge's measurement, with no room for opinion about the result.
A personal best is the best result a performer has achieved; a season's best is the best result in the current season.
Recording these results allows a performer to set measurable goals, such as improving a personal best by a stated amount.
Comparing results over sessions shows whether a training plan is working, which is the basis of performance analysis (studying performance to find strengths and weaknesses) in athletics.
Results are also compared with the achievements of others, so a performer can see where their standard sits in relation to a national or event standard.
notes.tip: Link the measurement to its use: because times and distances are objective, improvement is easy to record and compare, which suits goal setting and performance analysis.

notes.b: Each result must be fair and accurate, so athletics uses officials with set jobs. Knowing who does what is also part of the rules and conventions you are assessed on.
points: The starter controls the start of running events and enforces the false start rules (a false start is leaving before the start signal).
Track judges watch the lanes and the finish of running events, so that athletes stay in their lane and the finishing order is decided fairly.
Field judges measure every throw and jump and check each attempt for fouls (attempts that break the rules and do not count).
Timekeepers or electronic timing record the times of running events, so the result is a measurement and not an opinion.
Field events allow a set number of attempts for each athlete, so every competitor gets the same chances, and the high jump has its own elimination rule.
notes.tip: A question on rules and officials expects the starter and false starts, lane rules, track judges, field judges who measure and check fouls, timekeepers or electronic timing, and the number of attempts in field events.

notes.h: Safety common to all athletics events
notes.b: Throwing implements, spikes (shoes with metal points for grip) and hard landings all carry risk. These safety rules apply across athletics and are part of what you are assessed on.
points: Warm up thoroughly before any event, including the muscles that will be used most in the event, to prepare the body for hard effort.
Throwing areas are cleared before a throw and controlled throughout: athletes throw only on command and retrieve implements only on command.
Nobody walks across a throwing sector (the marked area where throws land) while throws are being made.
Discus and hammer are thrown from cages, which must be in place before throwing starts, so that a stray throw is contained.
Landing pits are raked and mats are in place before any jump, so the athlete lands on a prepared surface.
Spikes are checked for damage before a session, because damaged spikes can cause a slip or injury.
Implements must be of the correct weight for the age of the athletes, so that younger athletes are not given loads too heavy to control safely.
notes.tip: For a safety answer, cover the warm-up, clearing and controlling the throwing area, cages, raked pits and mats, spike checks and correct implement weight for age.

notes.b: The assessment pulls the earlier blocks together. You are assessed on one event, chosen within one category, as a whole performer and not only on how far or fast you go.
points: The assessment is of one event, chosen within one category.
It covers the listed skills and techniques of that event.
It covers the rules and conventions of the event (the accepted ways of competing), and the safe practice that goes with it.
Technique for each event is taught in the notes for that category, not here, because each category has its own techniques.
notes.tip: Do not describe event technique in answers about the athletics area in general. Each category has its own notes for that.

notes.h: Athletics as a context for theory
notes.b: The same principles from the theory chapters recur across the athletics events, so athletics is used as a named activity in written answers. Each point below names the principle and the event it fits.
points: Energy systems (the ways the body makes the energy for muscles): a 100 m sprint draws mainly on the ATP-PC system, and a 400 m race mainly on the lactic acid system with a large aerobic contribution.

A 10,000 m race draws mainly on the aerobic system (the one that uses oxygen), because the effort lasts long enough for oxygen to supply the energy. There is more on this in the note titled Energy systems.
Levers and Newton's laws: a throw or jump is explained by a lever (a rigid bone turning about a joint) whose end speed depends on a straight, long arm or leg.
Newton's third law (every force has an equal and opposite reaction) applies too, since the ground reaction force from the take-off propels the athlete.

Planes and axes: the turns of a discus or hammer thrower are rotation in the transverse plane (a flat horizontal slice through the body) about the longitudinal axis (an imaginary line running from head to toe).

Fitness components and testing: a 10,000 m race depends on aerobic endurance (keeping going for long periods), a shot-put throw depends on muscular strength and power, and a 100 m sprint depends on speed.
Periodisation (dividing the training year into phases): general conditioning comes first, then event-specific training, with the peak timed for the main competitions.
notes.tip: Athletics is a frequent context in past papers. Be ready for a sprinter's practice principles, the discus and hammer planes and axes, the javelin's lever and practice method, components of fitness for 10,000 m versus shot-put, and energy systems in running events.

keyTerms.definition: A group of running, jumping, throwing and walking events, performed indoors or outdoors, measured against the performer's own ability and against others' achievements.
The best result a performer has ever achieved in an event.
The best result a performer has achieved in the current season.
An official who measures throws and jumps and checks each attempt for fouls.
An official who watches the lanes and the finish of running events.
The official who starts running events and enforces the false start rules.
The assessment of one athletics event chosen from one category, covering its skills, techniques, rules and safe practice.
The marked area into which a throw must land to count.
A measurable result, such as a time or distance, that makes improvement easy to record and compare.

factCards.definition: Running, throwing and jumping; the learner selects one for the performance assessment.
Sprints, middle distance, long distance and hurdles.
High jump, long jump and triple jump.
The starter, track judges and timekeepers or electronic timing.
Field judges, who measure each attempt and check it for fouls.

questions.prompt: Outline three safety rules for a throwing event.
questions.model: First, the throwing area is cleared before any throw and athletes throw only on command, so nobody is in the sector when the implement is released. Second, implements are retrieved only on command and carried back to the thrower rather than thrown back, so nobody is struck returning them. Third, nobody walks across the throwing sector while throws are being made, so people stay behind the throwers and out of the landing area.

questions.prompt: Explain why athletics events suit performance analysis and goal setting.
questions.model: Athletics results are objective: a time or a distance is recorded exactly, so there is no room for opinion about the result. This allows the performer's improvement to be measured by comparing a personal best or a season's best with earlier results, and by comparing results across training sessions to see whether a training plan is working. Because each result is a precise number, a performer can set a measurable goal, such as improving a personal best by a stated amount, and check their progress towards it. The same numbers can also be compared with the achievements of others, so the performer can see where their standard sits.
